title: Rancor
summary: Rancor is a modest but persistent espionage activity set that public reporting, notably from Palo Alto Networks around 2018, has linked to a suspected Southeast Asian state sponsor with low to moderate confidence. The group's reported victims are concentrated in government and military related organisations in Southeast Asia, with occasional activity reported in other regions and against civil society. Its tradecraft is far less remarkable than its longevity: regional language spear phishing delivered through crafted documents and links, delivery of malware through common cloud file sharing services, and the use of publicly available remote access tools and downloaders that are easy to replace when they are discovered. Public reporting has described lure themes tied to regional politics and campaigning, and the group has repeatedly returned to the same victim organisations after a period of quiet. Evidence in an environment is mostly behavioural rather than signature driven: documents arriving from consumer file sharing links, contacts with newly registered domains, remote access utilities installed by user accounts, credential access activity on workstations, and frequent configuration changes to tooling. Investigators should note that public naming is inconsistent, that some reporting describes overlapping clusters, and that much of the tooling is shared with criminal actors. The common misunderstanding is that a group must be technically advanced to be dangerous; this one is dangerous because it is patient and reuses what works.

beginner.definition: Rancor is a name used for a spying group that is suspected of working for a state in Southeast Asia. Public reports describe it since around 2017. It does not use rare or famous hacking tools. Instead it sends simple messages to people in government and military organisations, over and over again.
beginner.whyItMatters: It is easy to ignore an attacker who looks unskilled. This group proves that patience matters more than cleverness. Its messages come from places people already trust, like shared documents. It also returns to the same targets after being cleaned out. If your team stops watching after a single clean-up, the next attempt may succeed.
howItWorks: The attacker picks a target organisation and studies its people and its work.
A message is sent in the local language with a theme that feels current and relevant.
The link points to a shared document service that most security tools allow.
Opening the document or link installs a small downloader on the computer.
The downloader fetches a remote access tool that gives the attacker control.
Stolen files and passwords are collected, and the attacker stays as long as possible.
beginner.example: Imagine a locksmith who never picks a lock. He knocks on the office door with a clipboard. He says he is there for the quarterly safety check and is waved through. The visit takes five minutes and nothing looks broken. He returns three months later and is recognised as a familiar face. Rancor behaves like that visitor. The technique is ordinary. The disguise is local and familiar, and the advantage comes from returning often enough that nobody questions the visit.
takeaways: Treat files and links from public sharing services as untrusted until you verify the sender.
Do not lower your guard after a clean-up, because repeat targeting is common.
Log which tools are normally installed, so unusual remote access software stands out.

objectives: Describe how abuse of legitimate file sharing services hides malicious delivery.
Explain why repeat targeting makes a low sophistication group a durable risk.
Identify the behavioural clues left by a downloader and remote access tool.
Explain why public naming and attribution for this group is uncertain.
Recommend controls that limit the value of stolen credentials and stolen files.
